title: The draft by the numbers
photoNote: President Roosevelt signs the Selective Training and Service Act, 16 September 1940. Public domain on Wikimedia Commons. Six weeks before the lottery.
body:
When the first number came out of the bowl, 6,175 men across America found out they held it.

29 October 1940. The lottery put into motion the Selective Training and Service Act, which President Roosevelt had signed on 16 September. It created the first peacetime draft in American history. Men from 21 to 35 registered. Those chosen served twelve months, no more than 900,000 could be in training at once, and they could serve only in the Western Hemisphere or American territory.

The one year limit did not last. In August 1941 the House voted to extend service by a single vote, 203 to 202. Four months later, the country was at war.
threads:
When the first draft number came out of the bowl, 6,175 American men found out they held it.

29 October 1940. Men 21 to 35 had registered for America's first peacetime draft. Those chosen would serve twelve months, no more than 900,000 at a time.

In August 1941 the House kept them in uniform longer by a single vote, 203 to 202.

declassified.fact: Even Stimson's blindfold had a pedigree. It was a strip of yellow linen cut from the upholstery of the chair used at the signing of the Declaration of Independence. After he drew the capsule, he handed it straight to Roosevelt to read out.
